result:
The proposed answer is almost certainly too large, because it only considers coplanar configurations.

**The 2D example is valid.** For A=(0,0,0), B=(k,k−1,0), C=(0,1,0), P=(k−1,k−2,0), the point P lies below line AB and so is outside T. The cross-product computation gives a distance of 1/√(k²+(k−1)²) to line AB. The projection of P onto AB falls inside the segment, so this is also the distance to T.

**Why it is not the minimum.** P does not have to lie in the plane of T. If P is off the plane and its projection lands inside T, then P∉T automatically, and the distance is the plane distance 1/|n|, where n is the primitive integer normal of the plane. Normals formed from edge vectors in [−k,k]³ can have length of order k², since the cross-product coordinates grow like k². That makes the distance order 1/k², far smaller than the coplanar value of about 1/(√2·k).

**Check at k=2.** Take u=(2,1,0) and v=(1,2,2). Their cross product is (2,−4,3), with norm √29, so a lattice point can lie at plane distance 1/√29≈0.186. The proposed formula gives 1/√5≈0.447 for k=2. I did not check that the projection falls inside the triangle for this particular example. The scaling argument is enough to show the 2D configuration is not optimal for larger k.

The proposed value is therefore not the true minimum.

VERDICT: REJECT
